crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Forecasting research trends in citation mapping and discovery means using the structure of scholarly references to spot which questions, methods, and communities are gaining momentum before they become obvious. The work covers emerging research fronts, rising authors and institutions, shifts in terminology, and the spread of ideas across disciplines. It treats citations not as simple endorsements but as traces of intellectual influence that can be read in aggregate. The goal is a forward-looking map of where a field is heading, grounded in the published record rather than in search popularity or social media attention.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practice runs on curated bibliographic databases, full-text repositories, and citation graphs built from publisher metadata and open scholarly records. Trend forecasting adds a temporal layer: snapshots of the citation graph at different dates, so that edges can be treated as events with timestamps. Storage is usually a graph database or a columnar store that can hold very large paper and reference collections, with batch jobs for recomputing network measures. The site's own collection of 135 research papers and 11,075 extracted claims is a small, carefully selected subset used for demonstration and validation, not the full corpus.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts begin by building a citation network from a seed set of papers and expanding through references and citing works. They then compute standard measures such as direct citation counts, co-citation clusters, and bibliographic coupling strength, often combined with keyword and abstract text. Burst detection flags terms or papers whose activity rises sharply relative to their own history, while network centrality identifies nodes that bridge otherwise separate clusters. Forecasts are usually made by extrapolating these signals over rolling time windows, comparing recent cohorts against older baselines, and checking whether a trend is broad based or driven by a single lab or venue.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is the main governance concern, because a trend forecast is only as good as the citation and metadata records behind it. Citation indexes have coverage gaps by language, region, and discipline, and they can overrepresent journals with strong digital metadata. Forecasts can also amplify early hype or create self-fulfilling attention around a paper, so the work distinguishes signal from manipulation such as citation rings. On this site, every claim links to the original paper rather than to a secondary search tool, which keeps the evidence chain short and auditable. Rights issues are mostly about access to full text and publisher metadata, not about the forecast itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The next stage is likely to combine citation structure with full-text argument mining, so that a trend is defined not only by who cites whom but by what specific claims are being reused, challenged, or extended. Large language models are making it cheaper to extract those claims at scale, though they introduce new risks of hallucinated references and need careful grounding in the source record. Another direction is live forecasting, where models update daily or weekly as new preprints and accepted papers enter the graph. The field is also moving toward uncertainty-aware forecasts that show how much a predicted trend depends on a few key papers or a single funding cycle.
